titleStmt.title: Schedulability analysis of multi-packet messages in segmented CAN

analytic.title: Schedulability analysis of multi-packet messages in segmented CAN

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The CAN bus is one of the most used networks in distributed real-time systems. The CAN bus can be divided by means of bridges in order to distribute the network load among different segments and contribute positively to the schedulability of the system. On the other hand, CAN supports the fragmentation of a message in multiple packets when it does not fit into one single CAN frame. The schedulability analysis of CAN has been extensively studied in the literature. Although the proposed methods analyze non-segmented CAN buses, they can be applied to segmented networks. However, the techniques from the related literature obtain quite pessimistic results in the analysis of segmented CAN networks with multipacket messages. This paper proposes a less pessimistic CAN schedulability analysis method for the mentioned kind of networks. Moreover, this optimized technique can be integrated with methods oriented to the holistic schedulability analysis of a complete distributed real-time system.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The CAN bus is one of the most used communication networks to connect distributed real-time systems. CAN is usually configured with a bus topology, but it can be divided by means of bridges [1] or gateways in order to form other topologies that distribute the network load in segments or domains [2]. These configurations are typical in the automotive communication systems, where each segment clusters the hardware and software related with different parts of the vehicle, e.g. powertrain domain, chassis domain, body domain, etc [3]. Moreover, the segmentation of the CAN network can make a distributed real-time system schedulable [4]. However, the network traffic of the segments is not always isolated. For instance, some automotive applications require the exchange of messages between different segments, e.g. the engine controller (powertrain domain) takes input from the climate control (body domain), the dashboard (body domain) displays information from other domains [3].

CAN is typically used to transmit small data quantities in single packets. However, there are mechanisms to fragment the messages that are longer than the maximum length of the CAN frame and send them in multiple packets. Sometimes, long messages such as big data blocks, long remote commands or logs may have to be transmitted between different segments of the CAN network, as shown in Section IV.

The schedulability analysis of the CAN bus has been extensively studied in the related literature. The current stateof-the-art method [5], which is used on the classical holistic schedulability analysis, is suitable for segmented CAN networks whose messages are not longer than the maximum length of the CAN frame. However, when messages have to be fragmented because they do not fit into one single packet, the mentioned schedulability analysis method is quite pessimistic in segmented CAN networks. The present paper proposes an optimized CAN schedulability analysis technique that obtains more accurate results than previous techniques in this type of systems.

This paper is structured as follows. Section II describes the related work. Section III discusses the system model. Section IV shows a realistic application that motivates the proposal. Section V explains the limitations of the holistic schedulability analysis techniques for segmented CAN with multi-packet messages. Section VI explains the optimized CAN schedulability analysis technique. Section VII shows the experiments and results. And finally, Section VIII outlines conclusions and future work.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Extensive research on the schedulability analysis of traffic on CAN has been carried out over the last two decades, most of which based on the earlier work of Tindell [6]. Subsequently, an enormous amount of analyses have been developed, covering diverse application scenarios and traffic models, from probabilistic analysis techniques that cope with errors [7] to the use of dynamic priorities [8], timetriggered communication [9], reduced stuffing jitter [10], etc. Later on, the work in [5] showed that the original Tindell's analysis was optimistic in a few situations and proposed the due corrections. The analysis of CAN continued generating interest in the research community as shown by the recent work in [11] that considers the FIFO behaviour of industrial CAN device drivers.

The segmentation of the CAN network has been applied in the automotive domain, but it has also been used in other more generic domains [4] and with different paradigms, like time-triggered networks [12], for instance. The fragmentation of messages longer than a single CAN frame is a well known mechanism implemented in high level protocols such as DeviceNet and CANopen. The timing issues related to the transmission of amounts of data larger than a single CAN frame can carry has been addressed in [13] by means of the utilization of a priority inheritance protocol to expand the non-preemptive nature of the packet transmissions to the whole message level.

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: The physical architecture of our system is composed of a CAN network that can be divided in segments by means of bridges. The logical architecture is based on the system model defined in [14] for the composition of heterogeneous scheduling techniques in distributed systems. An end-to-end flow Γ i is a linear sequence of steps τ ij that has an activation period T i and a deadline D i . Each step τ ij has a worst-case execution or transmission time C ij , an initial input jitter J ij due to local issues, e.g. accuracy of the clock, an initial offset Φ ij , a worst-case response time R ij , a best-case response time R b ij , an inherited input jitter J ij , and an inherited offset Φ ij , also known as the best-case release time.

A step τ ij can be a task or a message. A task can also be denoted by t ij . A message can also be denoted by m ij , and it is composed of one or more packets p ijk (k = 1, 2, ..., L), depending on whether it fits into a single CAN frame or not. The present proposal considers that a message traverses at most two segments. The source segment is the segment from which the message is sent, whereas the target segment is the segment to which the message is sent. C ijk is the worst-case transmission time of the packet p ijk . The inherited release jitter and the best-case release time of the message and its first packet are equal (J ij = J ij1 and Φ ij = Φ ij1 ). Similarly, and being p ijL the last packet of the message, the best and the worst-case response times of the message and its last packet are also equal (R b ij = R b ijL and R ij = R ijL ). For the sake of simplicity, a lower bound on the best-case response time is computed as the sum of the best-case execution and/or transmission time of the current task, message and/or packet and all the previous ones in the end-to-end flow.

div.head: IV. MOTIVATING APPLICATION
div.p: This section shows a realistic automotive example with multi-packet messages that cross different segments. Figure 1 illustrates the Scenario 1 (Sc1) and the tables in Figure 2 show the characteristics of the applications (end-to-end flows), tasks and messages. The bigger the number, the higher the priority. In the Γ 1 application, the information captured by an array of radars located in the chassis domain is clustered and transmitted by the task t 11 through a bridge towards the body domain in order to be displayed in the dashboard of the vehicle by the task t 14 . There are 4 shortrange radars for the parking assistance in each side of the vehicle, giving a total number of 16. Moreover, there are 8 medium-range radars for the detection of more distant obstacles around the vehicle. Hence, there are a total number of 24 radars, each one of them giving 3 bytes of data: 1 for the identification of the concrete radar, 1 for the distance of the obstacle, and 1 for the speed of the obstacle. Therefore, the obstacle map around the vehicle created and transmitted by the task t 11 located in the computer ECU 1 is composed of 24 x 3 = 72 data bytes. Additionally, a timestamp of 6 bytes is appended to the obstacle map, so it has 78 bytes that have to be transmitted in message m 12 through the segment of the chassis domain and m 13 through the segment of the body domain. A CAN packet can transport at most 8 data bytes, so the obstacle map has to be fragmented in order to be transmitted in multiple packets. Each packet uses 1 byte for the identification of the message, 1 byte for the identification of the fragment, and the remaining 6 bytes to carry the information of the obstacle map. Therefore, 78 / 6 = 13 packets are required to transmit all the obstacle map, resulting in a data length of 13 x 8 = 104 bytes.

The applications Γ 2 and Γ 3 execute completely in the chassis and body domains, respectively, and consist of a periodic capture made by Sensor2 and Sensor3 processed by tasks t 21 and t 31 , which transmit the single-packet messages m 22 and m 32 to tasks t 23 and t 33 in order to carry out the corresponding actuation with Actuator2 and Actuator3, respectively.
This CAN network uses the extended CAN frame of 128 bits and a baudrate of 500 Kbits/s, so the worst-case transmission time (WCTT) of each packet is 0.256 ms.

div.head: V. LIMITATIONS OF HOLISTIC SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS FOR SEGMENTED CAN
div.p: As previously mentioned, the CAN network can be segmented by means of bridges in order to make a distributed real-time system schedulable [4]. Each segment of the network is a schedulable resource that can be analyzed independently. When all CAN messages fit into single CAN frames, the current holistic CAN technique can analyze segmented CAN networks properly. However, when CAN messages do not fit into single CAN frames and thus they have to be fragmented in packets, the holistic analysis method can be quite pessimistic. The origin of this pessimism lies in the consideration of the message as an atomic schedulable entity, ignoring the packetization and entailing that the message cannot be transmitted through the output port of the bridge until it has been received completely -all the packets-from the source segment. Put in another way, the holistic schedulability analysis method considers that packets that have arrived at the bridge need to wait for the other packets of the message that have not yet arrived at the bridge. However, the real system behaves as a pipeline, so a packet already in the bridge does not wait and is immediately allowed to compete for transmission through the output port. The difference between the results of both approaches can be clearly seen in the following example.

Scenario 2 (Sc2) is composed of a CAN network divided in 2 segments. There is only one message called A that is fragmented into 10 packets. For the sake of clarity, the worstcase transmission time of each packet is 1 ms. as in the example described in [5]. Message A is transmitted from a node in Segment 1 (S1) to another node in Segment 2 (S2). Figure 3 corresponds to this system and shows the diagrams of a) the real situation and b) the approach of the holistic analysis. As can be seen, the pipelining causes the message to have a real end-to-end worst-case response time of 11 ms. By contrast, current holistic schedulability analysis techniques [5] give a very pessimistic result of 20 ms.

A. Precedence relations
div.p: The higher accuracy of the optimized CAN schedulability analysis is achieved by considering the real precedence relations between the packets that cross different segments, which allow us to bound their release times more tightly. These precedence relations go beyond the traditional linear model used in single-segment CAN, and consequently, some Example 2, stand-alone new factors have to be defined and some classic concepts need to be rewritten. div.head: B. Critical instant
div.p: The critical instant is the moment at which a step is released along with all the steps of higher priority that can execute simultaneously. Just an infinitesimal moment before the critical instant the processing resource is free, so the step could start executing if higher priority steps would not activate. The worst-case response time of a step is calculated by creating the critical instant for that step.

In the source segment, the worst-case response time of any packet of a message is computed from the critical instant of the first packet of the message. However, in the target segment and due to the precedence relations, the worst- case response time of any packet may be the response time computed from the critical instant of the first, an intermediate, or the last packet of the message. This statement is shown with the Scenario 3 (Sc3) in Table I and Figure 4. This example is composed of a CAN network divided in 2 segments and 3 multi-packet messages. Message A is transmitted only through segment S1 whereas message B only through segment S2. By contrast, message C is transmitted from S1 to S2. The larger the priority number, the higher the priority. The time diagrams are drawn in the figure, where the activations of the messages are represented by downward arrows. In the target segment (S2), only the worst-case response time of the last packet of the message is computed because this is the one that triggers the next step in the end-to-end flow.

div.p: In case a) of Figure 4, when the first packet C1 and the last packet C5 arrive at S2 and try to be transmitted, message B of higher priority is released, creating a critical instant with C1 and/or C5 for message C and resulting in an optimistic -so invalid-worst-case response time (WCRT) of 15 ms. for C. C3 doesn't create a critical instant because C2 isn't sent yet. On the contrary, in case b), message B is released when the intermediate packets C2 and C4 try to be transmitted through S2, creating a critical instant with C2 and/or C4 for message C and resulting in a worst-case response time of 16 ms. for C. Therefore, in this scenario, the worst-case response time of C in S2 has to be computed creating the critical instant with the intermediate packets C2 and/or C4.

However, we have found other scenarios where the worstcase response time of the message C in the target segment has to be computed creating the critical instant with the first or the last packet. These examples, which are not included due to space limitations, show that the proper packet used to create the worst case critical instant in the target segment is unknown in advance. Therefore, the worstcase response time of a message in the target segment is the largest one among the different response times resulting from the different critical instants created with each packet of the target segment. This forces us to know the worst-case release times of all the packets of the target segment, which mandatorily requires calculating the worst-case response times of all the packets of the source segment.

div.head: C. Busy period
div.p: The schedulability analysis of a step requires the computation of the busy period, denoted by the symbol ω busy ab and defined as the time interval in which the processor or network is busy executing steps with priorities equal to or higher than the step τ ab under analysis [15].

In non-preemptive real-time systems, the busy period of the step under analysis contains Q ab instances of the step [5], so all of them have to be analyzed. In the present problem, a full message is considered as the step under analysis despite the fact that we are analyzing its individual packets. Equation (4) shows the expression to calculate the number of instances Q ab of message m ab in the busy period:
div.formula: Q ab = ω busy ab + (J ab + Φ ab ) Ta(4)
div.p: where ω busy ab is the busy period of the message m ab , (J ab + Φ ab ) is the worst-case release time of the message m ab , and T a is the activation period of the end-to-end flow Γ a .
The busy period is computed with the recurrence relation in Equation ( 5), starting with ω busy 0 ab = C ab , and finishing when ω busy n+1 ab = ω busy n ab :
div.formula: ω busy n+1 ab = B ab + ∀m ij ∈hep(m ab )     ω busy n ab + J ij + Φ ij Ti     • Cij (5)
div.p: where B ab is the blocking caused by the longest packet with a lower priority than m ab , and hep(m ab ) is the set of messages with priorities equal to or higher than m ab .

div.head: D. Interference
div.p: The interference term is the time interval in which an active step cannot execute because other higher priority steps are active. The worst-case response time of a step depends on the interference term, among other factors.

The interference caused by a packet p ijk over a lower priority packet during a time window of ∆t and considering that the packet p ijY is the one released at the critical instant is computed with Equation (6): where (x) 0 = max(x, 0) and H is the Heaviside step function, whose definition is Equation ( 7):
div.formula: I ijY ijk (∆t) = ∆t + (J ijY + Φ ijY ) -Φ ijk Ti + H[Φ ijk -Φ ijY ] 0 • C ijk
div.p: There are two possible cases depending on the differences between the best-case release time of the interfering packet p ijY with which the critical instant is created (Φ ijY ) and the best-case release time of any other interfering packet (Φ ijk ): when Φ ijk < Φ ijY and when Φ ijk ≥ Φ ijY .

These two scenarios are shown in Figure 5, where t c = J ijY + Φ ijY is the critical instant, p ijk is any interfering packet, ∆t is the time interval in which the network is busy transmitting packets, white portions in ∆t are the interferences caused by p ijk , and shaded portions in ∆t are transmissions of higher priority packets not shown in the figure . As can be seen, the interference caused by any packet p ijk is calculated in a situation where p ijY is released at its worst-case release time (J ijY +Φ ijY ), which is considered as the critical instant, and the interfering packet p ijk is released with its period T i and best-case release time (Φ ijk ). As mentioned in Section III, the best-case response time of a packet is computed as the sum of the best-case transmission and/or execution times of the current packet and all the previous steps in the end-to-end flow. This implies that, in the best case, all the packets of a message are transmitted one after the other without any time gap between them, i.e. as a complete message. As can be seen in Figure 5 with p ijk , the best case is considered for the interfering packets, i.e. they are activated with their best-case release times. Therefore, from the point of view of the packet under analysis, all the higher priority packets of a message are transmitted as a complete message. Accordingly, if as in the present approach trivial lower bounds for the best-case response times are used, the higher priority packets are considered to be transmitted as complete messages. Therefore, the first packet of the message is considered to be released at the critical instant, i.e. p ijY = p ij1 , and the interference is I ij1 ijk (∆t).

div.head: E. Execution window
div.p: The execution window is the time interval inside the busy period that extends from the release instant of the step under analysis to the finalization of the execution of the same or another instance of that step. The execution window ω abY abc (q) of a packet p abc with the packet p abY released just at the critical instant is computed with the recursive Equation ( 8):
div.formula: ω abY n+1 abc (q) = B abc + ∀p abc ∈m ab q • C abc + p abc-1 p abe =p abY C abe + ∀m ij ∈hp(m ab ) ∀p ijk ∈m ij I ij1 ijk ω abY n abc (q)(8)
div.p: where q = 0, 1, ..., Q ab -1 is the instance of the packet p abc under analysis inside the busy period, B abc is the blocking caused by the longest packet of lower priority, and hp(m ab ) is the set of messages with priorities higher than m ab . The first summation adds the worst-case transmission times of previous instances of the message, considering all its packets. The second summation adds the worst-case transmission times of the packets between the one released at the critical instant and the packet under analysis. Note that in the second summation of Equation ( 8) the worst-case transmission time of the packet under analysis is not added. This is due to the fact that the packet cannot be preempted once it starts to be transmitted, so all the packets with higher priority released during this interval do not contribute to the width of the execution window of the packet under analysis. The last summation adds the interferences caused by all higher priority packets. Equation ( 8) is explained by means of the following example.

Figure 6 shows the Scenario 4 (Sc4) composed of a message m ab with two packets p ab1 and p ab2 , and a higher priority message m ij with one packet p ij1 . Message m ab is activated with a period T a , and packets p ab1 and p ab2 are released with their worst-case release times J ab1 + Φ ab1 and J ab2 + Φ ab2 , respectively. Dark grey portions are interferences caused by transmissions of the higher priority packet p ij1 , whereas light grey portions are delays caused by the transmission of packets of message m ab . Both the higher priority packet p ij1 and the instance q = 0 of p ab1 are released at the critical instant t c with their corresponding worst-case release times. At this moment, p ij1 is transmitted and p ab1 waits. In the meanwhile, instance q = 0 of p ab2 is released and also waits. When p ij1 finishes, p ab1 is transmitted. After that, p ab2 is transmitted, but in the meantime, the instance q = 1 of p ab1 is released. When p ab2 finishes, p ab1 is transmitted, and the activation of the second instance of p ij1 occurred at its best-case release time has to wait because, despite having a higher priority, the CAN network is non-preemptive. When the second instance of p ij1 finishes, instance q = 1 of p ab2 would be transmitted, and so on. The number q of instances of the packets of message m ab that have to be checked is determined by the Q ab factor expressed in Equation (4).

div.head: F. Worst-case response time
div.p: As mentioned in Section VI-B, in the source segment the worst-case response times of all the packets of the message have to be calculated with the first packet released at the critical instant, p abY = p ab1 , as shown in Equation ( 12):
div.formula: R abc = max q=0,1,...,Q ab -1 ω ab1 abc (q) + C abc + (J ab1 + Φ ab1 ) -q • Ta(12)
div.p: On the other hand, in the target segment the only worstcase response time of the last packet p abL is calculated with different critical instants created with all the packets. The definitive worst-case response time is the largest one among them, as expressed in Equation ( 13):
div.formula: R abL = max q=0,1,...,Q ab -1 max Y =1,2,...,L ω abY abL (q) + C abL + (J abY + Φ abY ) -q • Ta(13)
div.p: Note that a quantity equivalent to the transmission time of the packet under analysis (C abc and C abL ) is added in both Equations ( 12) and ( 13) because it is not computed in the execution window.

div.head: VII. EXPERIMENTS
div.p: This section is divided in two parts. The first one is focused on the three scenarios exposed in Sections IV, V and VI-B, while the second part contains experiments carried out over more complex scenarios. Both parts show the more accurate results obtained by the optimized schedulability analysis technique with respect to the holistic method, and the second one also shows the time performance of the two techniques.

div.head: A. Simple experiments
div.p: Table II shows the worst-case response times of message m 12 in Sc1 (Figures 1 and2), message A in Sc2 (Figure 3) and message C in Sc3 (Figure 4 and Table I) calculated with different analysis methods. The numbers in column Exact are obtained by inspection. In these simple examples, the optimized technique obtains exact results, and as can be seen, they are much better than the ones computed by the classical holistic schedulability analysis method. Furthermore, the worst-case response time of Γ 1 in Sc1 calculated with the holistic method is 0.7 + 13.312 + 1 = 15.012 ms., which violates the deadline of 10 ms. By contrast, the optimized method gives a worst-case response time of 0.7 + 7.168 + 1 = 8.868 ms., meeting the deadline.

div.head: B. Complex experiments
div.p: The experiments described in this subsection compare the performance of the optimized and the classical holistic methods with different system loads. The used scenario is described in detail in order to make the experiments reproducible.

Scenario 5 (Sc5) described in Table III is composed of two segments and 20 messages. There are 5 local messages in each segment, and the remaining 10 messages cross the bridge from one segment to the other. The periods of the messages are tuned in order to obtain four different system load proportions of the crossing messages with respect to the local messages: 25%, 50%, 75% and 100% (with 100% there are no local messages). In each one of these system configurations, the periods of the messages are gradually decreased in order to increase the total system load while keeping the corresponding system load proportion between crossing and local messages.

In order to compare the results of different methods, we define the Improvement factor in Equation ( 14) as the average improvement of the worst-case response time obtained by the optimized schedulability analysis technique with respect to the classical holistic method:
div.formula: Improvement = ∀m ij ∈Crs R h ij Rij -1 card(Crs)(14)
div.p: where R h ij and R ij are the worst-case response times computed with the holistic and the optimized schedulability analysis techniques, respectively, Crs is the set of messages that cross the bridge, and card(Crs) is the number of messages in Crs.

Figure 7 shows the Improvement factor in Sc5 for different total system loads and system load proportions. As can be seen, the improvement is of approximately 25% when 100% of the traffic crosses the bridge, and between 20% and 25% in the remaining cases. Nevertheless, this improvement is obtained at the expense of a longer schedulability analysis process. As can be seen in Figure 8, the classical holistic method needs between 0.3 and 4 seconds approximately, whereas the optimized technique takes between 17 and 500 seconds, i.e. two orders of magnitude more time. This is expected since the holistic technique analyzes 10 crossing elements (messages), whereas the optimized method analyzes 550 crossing elements (packets).

In other more complex experiments with more crossing messages and that are not shown here due to lack of space, we have observed that the average improvement is of approximately 15% while the computation times remain in reasonable values (between 1.5 and 20 seconds for the holistic and between 74 and 2654 seconds for the optimized). The exposed results are representative of the performance of the technique.

In summary, the optimized schedulability analysis clearly obtains more accurate results than the classical holistic method. The influence of the proportion of the local and crossing system loads is not specially remarkable. The computational cost of the optimized method is higher, but limited and acceptable because the worst-case response-time analysis is usually made off-line.

div.head: VIII. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: The CAN bus can be divided with bridges to distribute the network load among different segments and contribute positively to the schedulability of the system. On the other hand, fragmentation into multiple packets is needed when a message does not fit into one single CAN frame. The schedulability analysis techniques developed so far give pessimistic results in the analysis of segmented CAN networks with multi-packet messages.

This paper proposes an optimized CAN schedulability analysis method for segmented CAN networks that takes into account the pipelining of the packets in the bridge. The experiments show that the proposed technique obtains more accurate results than the classical holistic analysis method, but at the expense of a longer schedulability analysis process. As future work, we plan to develop a tighter best-case response time analysis for this kind of systems.
